@graph.language_description:
Ungarinyin_x000d_ is the name of the people and their language and is known as heavy_x000d_ pronunciation. Ngarinyin is also the people and their language and is known as_x000d_ light pronunciation.  When people are speaking they use Ungarinyin_x000d_ to talk about themselves and their relationship to their environment.

Ngarinyin_x000d_ is very closely related to Wurla and they are linked together in the Native_x000d_ Title Area. There are more than 62 clan estates in Wanjina-Wilinggin-Wunggurr_x000d_ Native Title claim, which was awarded in 2004.

Ngarinyin_x000d_ includes the dialects: Wilawila, Wolyamidi, Guwidj, Wurla, Ola, Walar, Worla,_x000d_ Wula, Wuladja, Wuladjangari.

Ngarinyin_x000d_ country is generally associated with the western half of the Kimberley Plateau._x000d_ These are the Ngarinyin place names travelling roughly west to east. Gawulara_x000d_ (Napier Range), Walarra (New Mount Hart), Gambarrambal (Old Mount Hart),_x000d_ Dalandi (Silent Grove), Iminji (Imintji), Jilariba (Munja), Malbirri_x000d_ (Pantijan), Gubungarri (Mount Barnett), Waa (New Mount Elizabeth), Nyangudunda_x000d_ (Old Mount Elizabeth), Dodnan (Dodnun), Nyalanggunda (Gibb River Homestead),_x000d_ Umalagurdunda (Old Beverley Springs), Balamandarra (Gibb River), Darlngga_x000d_ (Drysdale River), Man.gurerri (Doongan), Marranbabidi (PrapPrap), Munuru (King_x000d_ Edward River Crossing), Gurrunggu (Mount House Homestead), Garrenji (Karunjie),_x000d_ Theda Station, Malambu  (El Questro), Marion Downs.

Alan Rumsey with David_x000d_ Mowaljarlai† developed the Ngarinyin orthography used by the Mowanjum Language_x000d_ Project and is a modified version of practical orthography developed by_x000d_ linguist Barry Blake.

Ngarinyin_x000d_ spellings include: Ungarinyin, Ngarinjin, Ungarinjin, Narrinyind.

@graph.language_description:
Marri Amu includes the coastal strip from just south of Nganthiwudi (Cape Scott) continuing south to Anggileni (Cape Dombey). To the north is Mendheyangal country, to the east is Marrithiyel country and to the south is Marri Tjevin country (Marett et al. 2013).
Marri Amu and Marri Tjevin are mutually intelligible and are classified by linguists as dialects of the same language. However, custodians of these languages regard them as being quite different and there are important social, geographic and cultural difference associated with 'being' Marri Amu or Marri Tjevin and speaking Marri Amu or Marri Tjevin (Long et al 2016)
-----
Marett, A., Barwick, L., & Ford, L. (2013), For the sake of a song: Wangga songmen and repertories, Sydney University Press, Sydney.
Long, M., Piyalam, A., Dumoo, A., Kungul, Y., Perdjert, D., Kundijl, A., Dumoo, M., Chula, M., Tchinbururr, V., Mullumbuk, M., Klesch, M., Kungul, D., Crocombe, M. & Wightman, G. (2016), Marri Ami and Marri Tjevin Plants and Animals, Aboriginal biocultural knowledge from the Moyle River, plains and coast, north Australia, Batchelor Institute Press, Batchelor NT, Australia.

Marri Tjevin country stretches from Nadirri near the mouth of the Moyle River, inland to Perrederr, Yendilil and Yenmilhi, and northward to Marri Amu country from Cape Dombey. Marri Amy country is bounded by Marri Ngarr country to the east, and Magati Ke country to the south (Marett et al 2013).

Marri Amu and Marri Tjevin are mutually intelligible and are classified by linguists as dialects of the same language. However, custodians of these languages regard them as being quite different and there are important social, geographic and cultural difference associated with 'being' Marri Amu or Marri Tjevin and speaking Marri Amu or Marri Tjevin (Long et al 2016)
-----
Long, M., Piyalam, A., Dumoo, A., Kungul, Y., Perdjert, D., Kundijl, A., Dumoo, M., Chula, M., Tchinbururr, V., Mullumbuk, M., Klesch, M., Kungul, D., Crocombe, M. & Wightman, G. (2016), Marri Ami and Marri Tjevin Plants and Animals, Aboriginal biocultural knowledge from the Moyle River, plains and coast, north Australia, Batchelor Institute Press, Batchelor NT, Australia.

Marett, A., Barwick, L., & Ford, L. (2014), For the sake of a song: Wangga songmen and repertories. Sydney University Press, Sydney.

@graph.language_description:
Wunambal Gaambera is spoken in the most_x000d_ north-westerly part of the Kimberley region. Wunambal and Gaambera are ‘very_x000d_ closely related’, with very little difference in pronunciation and some_x000d_ different words. Karadada et al. (2011) explains 'It is possible that there_x000d_ were some differences in the past, but in recent times these differences have faded'.

According to McGregor (1993) Wunambal and Gaambera_x000d_ are also closely related to the other north Kimberley languages, Kwini, Miwa_x000d_ and Yiiji and more distantly related to Worlaja, Ngarinyin and Worrorra.

The Wunambal Gaambera people received their_x000d_ Native Title determination – Wanjina Wunggurr Uunguu in 2011 (Karadada et al._x000d_ 2011) and now work together as one group with their country listed as the Uunguu_x000d_ Indigenous Protection Area. Their country covers 2.5 million hectares of land_x000d_ and sea in the north Kimberley region of Australia.

Country associated with Wunambal Gaambera (Karadada_x000d_ et al. 2011) extends from north of the Prince Regent River taking in Ngauwudu (Mitchell_x000d_ Plateau), Scott’s Strait and Gibulde (Cape Voltaire), and some inland_x000d_ countries. Some ‘clans’ also exploited the resources of the adjoining small_x000d_ islands, especially Wuuyurru (Bigge Island), Prudhoe Island, Corneille Island_x000d_ and Cassini islands although, apart from Wuyurru, these islands were not_x000d_ permanently inhabited. Other Wunambal Gaambera_x000d_ places are Punamii Uunpuu (Mitchell Falls), Kandiwal, Wung-gaarindjii (Katers_x000d_ Island), Jalandal, Banjal (Vansittart Bay), Garmbemirri, Wapenbe, Mungulalu_x000d_ (Anjo Peninsula) and Wargul Wargul (Bougainville Peninsula).

 The Wunambal Gaambera orthography used for_x000d_ the Mowanjum Language Project was developed by Therese Carr and Wilfred_x000d_ Goonack†. The orthography has been updated from the pronunciation guide in_x000d_ Uunguu Plants and Animals: Aboriginal biological knowledge from Wunambal_x000d_ Gaambera Country in the north-west Kimberley.

 

Wunambal spellings include: Wunumbal,_x000d_ Wunabal, Wunambul, Wunumbul, Wonambul, Unambal, Woonambal,_x000d_ Wunambullu, Wunumabal, Woonambal.

Gaambera spellings include: Gambera,_x000d_ Gamberre, Gambre.

@graph.language_description:
According_x000d_ to the Damimangari Aboriginal Corporation (2012) the Worrorra language has_x000d_ eight clan groups: Larrinyuwai, Arrbarlandi, Uminda, Unggarrang, Yawijabay,_x000d_ Uurnbun, Wurnbangkurwai and Ornnorrongoy, and together they are referred as the_x000d_ Dambimangari; Saltwater people. The Dambimangari people were awarded their_x000d_ Native Title Determination in 2011.

As_x000d_ explained in the Damimangari Healthy Country Plan (2012), Worrorra speaking_x000d_ families lived traditionally on and near the north-west Kimberley coast between_x000d_ “Ungarrang at the bottom of Kimbolton to Marlundum in the Prince Regent area”. Clendon (2014, p.2) in_x000d_ collaboration with Worrorran language custodians, confirms that “in the south, Worrorra country extended_x000d_ inland some 40 kilometres from the coast, and in the north, roughly some 60_x000d_ kilometres inland, and 50 or so kilometres up the Malanduma (Prince Regent_x000d_ River Region), from where it empties into the St. George Basin. This region_x000d_ includes the lower and middle reaches of Malanduma (Prince Regent River_x000d_ Region), Ngarlangkarnanya (St. George Basin) Ngayangkarnanya (Mt. Trafalgar)_x000d_ and Nubungarri (Mt. Waterloo). It includes the George Water and Arn Nowngoy_x000d_ (Glenelg River) and Iledda (Walcott Inlet). On the coast Worrorra country_x000d_ includes Wurroolgu (Augustus Island) as well as many other offshore islands,_x000d_ and Yawijaba (Montgomery Islands and reefs)”.

The_x000d_ Worrorra orthography that has been used throughout the Mowanjum Language_x000d_ Project is based on the orthography developed by Mark Clendon with Sam_x000d_ Umbagai†, Amy Peters†, Daisy Utermorrah†, Patsy Lulpunda† and Heather Umbagai†,_x000d_ however there have been several changes to the orthography over the last five_x000d_ years as requested by senior Worrorra speakers.

@graph.language_description:
Pumbah (footprints or walking tracks) encompass many travelling and trading routes across and through lok Koongurrukun (Koongurrukun country). There exists a loop that starts with wulwul jirruk, (Tumbling Waters) with its effervescent springs, mibi cober koormandum, (underground eyes of water) to embrace Luniook (Berry Springs) then across Panawulk at (Blackmore) and Nungulukoo (Finniss) Rivers and the important sites  in Purlugutj ( Litchfield National Park). Pumbah winds its way across and through the interior to take many pumbah to Annrukulpum (Rum Jungle) and into Ulmoolmi (Batchelor). While there are coastal pumbah the central location is Kurrinju.  The north-eastern boundary includes Lanji  (Darwin River), Tjetiring shared with the  Warai peoples near the area now known as Manton Dam. The pumbah networks travel south down through to Amulgul (Adelaide River. Helen Bishop 2017

Tindale: Koongurrukun Estate: Northeast of Mount Litchfield on midwaters of Reynolds River and on Adelaide River headwaters; an inland tribe extending to the western side of the Tabletop Range divide; northeast to vicinity of Rum Jungle and Batchelor.  http://archives.samuseum.sa.gov.au/tindaletribes/kungarakan.htm

@graph.biography: Killinang was born at Overn Station. Sometimes his family came to the Old Mission at Werntek Nganinyi to visit for rations and then they would go back to Wudipuli and Nama. After a while they stopped at the mission and Killinang went to school with his brothers. Killinang became a stockman working on stations at Kulchil, Tipperary, Litchfield and Wangi. Then he went back to Wadeye (Port Keats) for a while, but soon left to work at Victoria River Downs Campfield Station. He was mustering, fencing, and doing all the work of a stockman. He came back to Wadeye and got married. He also worked in gardens and in building trades. Killinang is famous for his dancing and for playing the didgeridoo. He travelled to Kununurra, Turkey Creek, Fitzroy Crossing and Derby as a dancer for ceremonies. Killinang was happy working at the language centre and taking part in ceremonies. He enjoyed hunting at Nama and sometimes at Kidenu or Nganbe.
@graph.title: Other

@graph.biography: Lungung Johnny Nama was born at Daly River but grew up at Dirrangara. His grandfather Tchinburrur was boss for Ma Muyil people. Before the war when he was a little boy he went to Old Mission (Werntek Nganinyi) with all his family, mother, father and grandfather. The family then went back to Dirrangara, but after a while they returned to Old Mission for tobacco and rations like sugar. They would travel back and forth from their country to Old Mission for tobacco and rations. During the war Lungung’s family decided to go back and stay at Old Mission and Lungung became a timber man, cutting stringy bark trees. He also travelled to Tipperary and Litchfield as a timber man, Lungung was married to Joan Pupuli and they had six children.
@graph.title: Other

@graph.biography: His father was going for kangaroo when he was a little boy, he went with his father. They went hunting to Mangure (Gibb River) downstream. Something about dreamtime there is a big Wadjina painting there Ngawera is the Wadjina at Donkey Creek. (Donkey creek that is their country) They walked and they walked, there were lots of watermelon. The station white-fellas he busted the watermelon, he opened it up and put poison for the dingo on the watermelon. His father found one watermelon already smashed and he ate the watermelon, his father died. Well he didn’t eat the watermelon and there he was a little fella maybe almost a teenager maybe 8-9yrs old. He walked back to Gibb Station and one woman found him walking on the airstrip, they asked where is your father and he said, no he is finished now. So he stayed there at Gibb River Stations and grew up to be a stockman.
@graph.title: Other

@graph.biography: Larri Rex Munar was born at Nganthamurri. He lived with his parents out in the bush. He would go hunting with his father and his father would tell him stories about their country. Larri worked as a stockman with Brother Quinn around Kura Chipmam, Kura Yipi, Kulchil and Palumpa Station. Later he came back to Wadeye (Port Keats) and got married to May Pupil. They had five children. Larri was happy working at the Wadeye Aboriginal Languages Centre and enjoyed taking the family to Nama and Wudipuli for bush holidays.
@graph.title: Other

@graph.biography: Maxie is the son of Mawanyngu Jeanie Jongmin and has lived all his life at Wadeye (Port Keats) and he has been painting for his clan group for many years. During the dry season, Maxie moves to Perrederr with his family for the bush holiday. When living at Perrederr he is hunting, looking for fresh water turtles and picking some bush tucker. The illustrations in A-Ngarryi Yagatiya contain elements from two of Maxie’s paintings about a-ngarryi yagatiya. The original art works are currently housed in the Kanamkek-Yile Ngala museum at Wadeye.
@graph.title: Other

@graph.biography:
Mark Crocombe has lived and worked at_x000d_ Wadeye for 35 years. Originally he was as a lay missionary employ by Pat Dodson_x000d_ and Fr Malcolm Fyfe to assist with taking people back to their country. Later_x000d_ the new community council Kardu Numida employed him and he has also been_x000d_ self-employed working with Elders in a community fishing business. It was_x000d_ during this period working with Elders that his interest in natural history,_x000d_ cultural stories and country was reignited and he began his journey of working_x000d_ in cultural preservation.  

In the mid 1980s Mark started working with_x000d_ researchers such as Les Hiddens and others to document bush tucker and bush_x000d_ medicine. As part of his cultural preservation work Mark undertook to document_x000d_ rock art of the region which he learnt as a young man travelling though central_x000d_ Queensland with his father.

Mark has been the Cultural Coordinator at Kanamkek-Yile Ngala_x000d_ Museum and Wadeye Aboriginal Languages Centre for a_x000d_ number of years, assisting in coordination documentation of languages and_x000d_ cultural knowledge. Today Mark is focused on digitisation of the Wadeye_x000d_ archives to ensure the preservation of video, audio, images and print_x000d_ resources. He has also become an expert photographer over the years and his_x000d_ images make a significant contribution to the Wadeye collection.

LeeAnne has worked in the field of education in the_x000d_ Northern Territory since 1985. She has worked at Batchelor Institute for the_x000d_ past twenty odd years and has participated in the production of many of the_x000d_ Batchelor Press publications in the CALL collection.

@graph.biography: Thomas is originally from Tasmania. He studied linguistics in Canberra and Perth. He is interested in endangered languages, especially Aboriginal languages of the western part of the Kimberley region of Western Australia. He has worked with speakers of a number of Kimberley languages including Ngarinyin and Worrorra. Thomas helped establish Worrorra arriarrganang (Worrorra revitalization project) with a Worrorra speaker at Mowanjum community in 2009. This project worked collaboratively with Batchelor Press to produce Worrorra language materials. In 2012 this work was expanded to include the related Ngarinyin and Wunambal languages and has since then operated as the Mowanjum Endangered Languages Program. Thomas has worked as the linguist on this program together with Batchelor Institute and members of Mowanjum Community including the Mowanjum Aboriginal Art and Culture Centre. Thomas has worked as a linguist for the Kimberley Language Research Centres and as a linguistic consultant. He has worked in the areas of Native Title, collaborated with scientists recording traditional ecological knowledge, indigenous land management (e.g. Indigenous Protected Area consultation), biological research and Aboriginal painting documentation. He lives in Broome.
@graph.title: Other

@graph.biography: Nganthamurri has lived at Wadeye (Port Keats) his whole life and is married with five children. He enjoys painting and coaching the Wudipuli Dockers football team in the wet season. Nganthamurri travels to his country at Wudipuli for hunting and to teach his children about their country. The illustrations in Muli Kanybubi Tjitjuk Kawuny Na Yagatiya contain elements from two of Nganthamurri’s paintings about Muli Kanbubi Tjitjuk Kawuny. The paintings are currently housed in Kanamkek-Yile Ngala museum at Wadeye.
@graph.title: Other

@graph.biography: Palibu was born at Palibu near Kuy and his early days were spent living with his family in their country. Palibu's father Parrmiri taught him fishing and his uncle Wilhi taught him how to hunt by himnself. Palibu was the youngest of eight children. He had five older sisters and two older brothers. In 1938 Palibu's family moved from Yederr to Werntek Nganinyi (OLd MIssion) where there were 700 Aboriginal people living together. Everyone at the mission worked clearing the jungle, planting gardens or building. In 1937 Palibu's family moved to Wadeye (Port Keats) where he worked as a timer cutter on teh bandsaw. Later he was a community health worker. During this period Palibu went on many long walking journeys to Daly River. He talked to Malak Malak, Wadjiginy and Tjemerri people, to tell them to love one another. He is known as 'The Peace Maker'. Palibu also travelled widely for ceremonies, dancing Wangga and later playing the didgeridoo. In 1942 he began work at Auvern Station as a stockman. He continued working there until he became sick with malaria in 1942, an was flown to Katherine Hospital. For his work at the staion he was given 1000 pounds in wages. From Katherine he took the train to Darwin. After a few days he was flown back to Wadeye on the medical plane. After that illness, Palibu regularly walked to Daly River and back to Wadeye, carrying material and bamboo spears for his parents. Palibu was away from the community for a long time for medical treatment. When he returned to the community he had a few weeks holiday and started work. He looked after the children in the dormitories and worked int eh Wadeye shop as a book-keeper for three years. He was then advised to finish work and go on the pension. In 1989 Palibu moved back to his homeland at Kuy to live with his wife and their children and his brother Gabriel Kungul and his family. The families had few resources. They contributed half of their pension to get solar power at their outstation. Palibu and his wife Mona live at Kuy for many years taking care of younger family members. Palibu advised the Wadeye community on issues of juvenile justice and caring for younger people when he was a member of the Thamarrurr Regional Council. He worked tirelessly to record and document his langauge and culture for his children, grandchildren and the generations to come.
@graph.title: Other

@graph.biography:
Alitj_x000d_ Ambrose Piyalam is also known as Purlda in his community. Pulda was his father’s_x000d_ brother’s name. Purlda was born at Ngindjirridi. He had a Marri Ngarr mother and_x000d_ father but he was brought up and taught Wangga by his uncle Munggum who was a_x000d_ famous Marri Tjevin song man. After his father died at Daly River, Purlda went_x000d_ to live with his uncle Ned Berida at Nadirri.

 

Purlda remembers dancing at Old Mission as a 12 year old. He quickly became famous as_x000d_ a dancer, performing Wangga, Lirrga, Malkarrin, Dharnpa, Wurlthirri (the song_x000d_ and dance genres of the Wadeye, Daly River region). He has danced at ceremonies_x000d_ at Palumpa, Peppiminarti, Daly River, Belyuen, and as far afield as Maningrida,_x000d_ Goulburn Island, Croker Island, Yarralin, Timber Creek, Kununurra, Turkey Creek_x000d_ and Fitzroy Crossing.

Purlda is famous for composing the Walakandha Wangga a-sjinmel, ‘Seagull Wangga’. Purlda worked in Father Docherty’s sawmill, build cattle yards and worked in the_x000d_ garden at Port Keats. Purlda worked as a senior language advisor not only_x000d_ in his own language but also assisting with Marri Tjevin.

@graph.biography:
Atu_x000d_ was born at Tjindi at Na Vebel. When he was a young teenager he left his_x000d_ parents at Perrederr and walked to Tjindi to stay with his auntie Kuwakwu_x000d_ Maggie Timber and his uncles Ditjpil and Gumbuduk. He was living in the bush_x000d_ learning from his family, travelling around his country. Father Docherty came_x000d_ to visit the family at Tjindi and asked them to move into the mission. The_x000d_ whole family walked away from Tjindi, all of the Rak Tulh mob. They went to Wadeye (Port Keats) when Atu was about 12 years old. He went to school at Port Keats._x000d_ They used slate and chalk to write, but Atu didn’t learn much about reading and_x000d_ writing English because he was thinking about his country. Atu ran away from_x000d_ Port Keats school. Twice he went back to his country. The third time he went to_x000d_ Tipperary where he was working with old men from Peppimenarti. Atu also worked_x000d_ at Litchfield and Finnis River stations as a stockman. Then he married Rosie_x000d_ Bengat Gaden, at Knucky’s Lagoon before Cyclone Tracy. After Cyclone Tracy the_x000d_ family went to Port Keats and lived at Perrederr, Nadirri and Tjindi, going_x000d_ fishing and living off the country. Later they moved back to Knucky's Lagoon_x000d_ for medical attention for Atu’s wife. After his death, his wife Rosie and the family moved back to Wadeye. 

Atu_x000d_ was famous for his dancing of Wangga, Lirrga and Thanpa. He traveled all round_x000d_ the country, Tjindi, Nadirri, Perrederr and Wadeye. He  also travelled to_x000d_ Gunbalanya, Warruwi, Belyuen, Kununarra, Derby, Kalumburu, Timber Creek and_x000d_ Balgo taking the young men for ceremonies. He was the businessman for those ceremonies because he was Ma Narrambu-leader for the ceremonies. 

Atu was famous for teaching the ceremonies, culture, stories and language for Ma_x000d_ Thanggurral. In Ma Thanggurral there are two clans Lhambu Tjendi comprising the_x000d_ Dumoo and Kundjil families; and Lhambu Brinkin, consisting of the Mullumbuk,_x000d_ Kanggiyang and Berida families.

Atu has also been an advisor for the Northern Land Council, an interpreter for the_x000d_ Supreme Court and a senior consultant for the mining industry.

Kampawerr_x000d_ Patricia Karui (nee Walanh) was born and grew up on the Mardanungamme estate._x000d_ As a baby, her mother Arna carried her wrapped up in paper-bark. In about 1932,_x000d_ Kampawerr’s family was camped at Purnpurn, when two policemen and a tracker_x000d_ came looking for the famous warrior Nemarluk. The police took Kampawerr’s_x000d_ father, Walanh from the family, although he was innocent of the crime he was_x000d_ blamed for. Because the police took most of the men from Mardanungamme, all the_x000d_ families had to move and nobody was left living on the Mardanungamme estate._x000d_ Kampawerr’s family moved to Auvergne Station after her father and uncles were_x000d_ taken away by the police.

When_x000d_ the Japanese bombed Darwin in 1942, all the prisoners were released from jail_x000d_ and they walked back to Port Keats Mission (Wadeye). Then Kampawerr’s father_x000d_ and others walked to Auvergne Station to reunite with their families. The_x000d_ family then walked to Port Keats Mission. When they got to the Mission, Father_x000d_ Richard Docherty came to their camp and talked to Kampawerr’s parents about her_x000d_ living in the dormitory with other young girls who were being looked after by_x000d_ the nuns. Kampawerr was lonely and homesick in the dormitory so she ran back_x000d_ home, but Father Docherty came to her camp and took her back to the convent. On_x000d_ Saturdays the girls’ parents came to visit and on Sundays Father Docherty would_x000d_ take them to the beach, or sometimes the girls would walk to Yawu or Kumewath. 

Kampawerr married Karui_x000d_ Thomas Karui and they had ten children. Today, Kampawerr works with the Wadeye_x000d_ Aboriginal Languages Centre telling stories about her country, the dreamings_x000d_ and taking family members to their country to teach them about their ancestry_x000d_ and country.

Tjakul_x000d_ was born at Tjindi on the Moyle River. Tjakul’s grandfather was Niwilhi Charlie_x000d_ Brinken Barbi who was a famous painter and songman. Tjakul was a young child_x000d_ when he came to live at Wadeye (Port Keats). During his working life he travelled the_x000d_ country and had many occupations including stockman, timberman, crocodile_x000d_ shooter, deckhand on the Margaret Mary, and he also worked at the Royal_x000d_ Australia Air Force base in Darwin. Tjakul was well known for making spears for_x000d_ old people and his singing and dancing for ceremonies.

Tjerrwurdi_x000d_ Mary Jongmin (Pulda) was born at Tjerrwurdi but lived at Kungarlbarl. She was_x000d_ promised to Bob Jongmin and she went with him to Daly River where she was_x000d_ crocodile shooting.

_x000d_ _x000d_ _x000d_ _x000d_ _x000d_ _x000d_ _x000d_ _x000d_ _x000d_ _x000d_ _x000d_ _x000d_ _x000d_ _x000d_ _x000d_ _x000d_ _x000d_ _x000d_ _x000d_ _x000d_ _x000d_ _x000d_ _x000d_

Tjerrwurdi_x000d_ travelled to many places crocodile shooting with her husband and his other_x000d_ wives, Jeannie, Maggie and Josephine. After many years they went to Palumpa and_x000d_ then to Kulchil. Finally, the family went to Port Keats where Tjerrwurdi lived for the rest of her life.

Tjinbili_x000d_ Anthony Nemarluk was born at Wadeye. He worked as a health worker for some time_x000d_ before moving to the housing industry in repairs and maintenance. Tjinbili is a_x000d_ family man, minding his children while his wife Miriam is teaching at the_x000d_ school. He has been working part-time for Wadeye Aboriginal Language Centre._x000d_ Tjinbili studied environmental health with Batchelor College and completed a_x000d_ Certificate in Environmental Health.

On_x000d_ completion of his studies he decided to concentrate on painting his dreams._x000d_ Tjinbili’s pantings have been sent to America, Sydney and Melbourne.

Yawa_x000d_ Edward Nemarluk Yawa was born at Tjind and lived there as a young child. When_x000d_ the community was at the Old Mission, only the men went to the mission for tea,_x000d_ sugar and tobacco. When the mission moved from Old MIssion to Wadeye (Port Keats), Yawa went to_x000d_ school. Later in his teenage years he was at Channel Island. When he_x000d_ returned to Port Keats he married and worked as a gardener until moving to the_x000d_ outstation at Nadirri. Much later he started his own outstation at his homeland_x000d_ Tjindi.

@graph.biography:
Donna has worked in a range of jobs,_x000d_ including teacher, teacher-linguist, graphic designer, newspaper journalist,_x000d_ technical writer and real estate agent.

_x000d_ _x000d_

In the 1980s she lived and taught_x000d_ in Arhnemland at Galiwin’ku and Warruwi, at a time when it was possible to_x000d_ experience the full richness of traditional Aboriginal cultures and languages_x000d_ before they quickly began to disappear. In the 1990s she moved to Batchelor_x000d_ Institute where she worked as regional lecturer, training Indigenous teachers_x000d_ in the Barkley Region and later in North West and North East Arnhemland.

_x000d_ _x000d_

She became involved with the_x000d_ endangered language project between 2002 -2004 after transferring to the_x000d_ Institute’s Curriculum and Research Unit (CARU). Working with Maree Klesh_x000d_ (Project Manager), Elizabeth Ford (Linguist) and Wadeye elders, Donna_x000d_ illustrated the first four books in the Dreamtime series: Mermaid Dreaming,_x000d_ Hairy Cheeky Yam, Emu Dreaming and Crocodile Dreaming. These books are now part_x000d_ of the CALL collection and serve as a permanent record of the sacred stories_x000d_ passed down by elders in the endangered languages of Marri Ngarr and Marri Amu._x000d_ Donna now lives in the Cairns area and continues to work as a teacher and_x000d_ graphic designer.

@graph.biography:
Aputh was born at Wadeye and_x000d_ went to school at Wadeye before attending Kormilda College. When he first_x000d_ started at Kormilda he went with Leon Melpi, Gordon Chula, Timmy Dumoo, Alfonso_x000d_ Kungul and Luke Bunduck. He finished Yr 12 at Wadeye.

_x000d_ _x000d_

 

_x000d_ _x000d_

His first job was as a hygiene_x000d_ worker for Wadeye Council and then he went to the Guisell Centre and studied_x000d_ construction and building for six months. He also learnt about plumbing,_x000d_ pottery and other trade skills. On completion of this course he became a_x000d_ construction worker for Wadeye Council.

_x000d_ _x000d_

 

_x000d_ _x000d_

From Council work he moved to_x000d_ the school and became part of the Literature Production Centre (LPC) team where_x000d_ he had his first taste of producing illustrations for Murrinh Patha books.

_x000d_ _x000d_

 

_x000d_ _x000d_

After he married he moved to_x000d_ the Wadeye clinic , but in 1983 he went back to the LPC in the old demountable_x000d_ at the school. The new LPC team was Aputh, Mempi Bede Lantjin, Dittin Alo_x000d_ Kungul, Pinpirrith Majella Chula, Mirkun Miriam Nemerluk (Bunduck), Mayirri_x000d_ Damien Tunmuck and Sr Tess Ward. In those days all the books were produced in_x000d_ black and white off a gestetner machine. It was operated by Mayirri who was_x000d_ often covered in ink from the tips of his fingers to his elbows.

_x000d_ _x000d_

 

_x000d_ _x000d_

Aputh, Mayerri and Bruce_x000d_ Tchinburrurr went to study printing and language studies at Batchelor College,_x000d_ and learned how to use an offset printer. The first colour book produced by the_x000d_ LPC was Ku Kananturturt (1985 ), with the then LPC manager Alan_x000d_ Karslake. It was a story about a little gecko.

_x000d_ _x000d_

 

_x000d_ _x000d_

Aputh continued to make_x000d_ Murrinh Patha language resources until 2001. He decided to go out bush and live_x000d_ on his Country to help look after the petrol sniffers and get them on the road_x000d_ to recovery. He had up to 30 young men at a time and worked with them to reconnect_x000d_ with culture and Country. The young men would stay on the outstation for 12_x000d_ months at a time and this continued until Opal fuel was introduced to Wadeye.

_x000d_ _x000d_

 

_x000d_ _x000d_

Aputh went back to work at_x000d_ the school, and from 2002-2007 he taught language to junior primary students; and_x000d_ did interpreting and translating for the non-Indigenous teachers.

_x000d_ _x000d_

 

_x000d_ _x000d_

Before retirement he took the_x000d_ position of Chairperson for the TRAACS Organisation at Wadeye and was also a Community_x000d_ Advisor. Aputh is now retired and lives on his Country for the dry season. His_x000d_ main goal is to spend time with his grandchildren on the weekends, teaching_x000d_ them about their culture, Country, hunting and fishing, and making sure they_x000d_ keep their language and culture strong.

@graph.biography:
Koormundum (Ida Edwards) was born in Darwin Hospital on 1st August 1926 to Harry and Poordjetpudjen (Margaret Edwards). Poordjetpudjen was the only daughter of Kungarakan matriarch, Ulynudubbu (Lucy), and Irishman Stephen McGuiness who immigrated to Australia as a young man in his early twenties. Lucy and Stephen had four other children, Barney, John (Jack), Val and Joe McGuinness, who are the forefathers of many Kungarakan. 

_x000d_

As the only girl in their clan, prior to his death in 1917, Stephen arranged for his friend, Harry Edwards to marry Poorjetpudjen in 1919. This was primarily to avoid her fate under the laws that governed the lives of Aboriginal people at that time. The first few years of Ida’s life was spent in a corrugated iron home in Woods Street, Darwin, then in a humpy at Darwin River where Harry worked a family tin mine named “The Lucy Claim”. Some of Koormundum first and fondest memories were of her Grannie, Lucy from whom she learned Kungarakan language as a child. Due to the chronic ill-health of her father Harry, he and his family moved south to Melbourne. Her father’s passing a few years later left Koormundum and her mother stranded from their much-loved country and family in the North. 

_x000d_

Koormundum continued and finished her education in Melbourne, graduating from Stotts Business College at the age of 19 with a Diploma in Business. She was employed as bookkeeper and typist. In her spare time she played violin in a string quartet as and was a member of the church choir. In 1952, Ida married a man she’d met at choir, Graham Bishop. Graham’s job as a school teacher took them all over the country and to territories like Christmas Island and the ACT. It was in Canberra when she applied to the Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies for a grant to help fund her ongoing and continued work on Kungarakan language. For the next 30 years’ she would document the language and history of her Kungarakan people and self-publish ngun Koongurrukun: Speak Koongurrukun, in 2000. 

_x000d_

Whilst many years were spent moving for work and raising six children, Koormundum never lost sight of her identity and role as a Kungarakan woman. Through the years, she kept in regular contact with her NT-based family and, even after her book was published, continued to research and advocate for Kungarakan people. She attended and gave evidence to the Finniss River Land Claim hearings in the early 1980s. She prepared vital evidence, maps and genealogies with her Elders and cousins, ultimately Kungarakan winning their case with their land restored them. 

_x000d_

Ida was an avid reader and writer. She wrote poetry and short stories. Her numerous notebooks record details anyone else may have missed or ignored. Ida’s love of words and language made her a great communicator, known to strike up conversations with strangers just to have a chat, regardless of where she happened to be. It didn’t seem to matter that she couldn’t speak their language, people always seemed to understand her. These traits made her the ideal language champion. 

_x000d_

Ida’s life work is her legacy, she did what was within her power to do, to keep Kungurrukun language alive. 

_x000d_

This work was dedicated to her mother Poordjetpudjen in keeping her promise to preserve Koongurrukun language. This enormous work is also Koormundum’s ngirrwut, the transferring of her knowledge, faithfully to all Koongurrukun to be understood from its own cultural basis and the very essence of Koongurrukun identity. Sadly, Koormundum passed away on 20th April 2014 her identity and her work gained us back our language. Her land rose up through surviving speakers so that she could hear it once more and return it to the people so it may speak through them once again. 

 Prepared by her children, Anthony, Katherine, Helen, Barbara, Andrew and Meg.

@graph.biography: Djalarra Stanley Rankin works in the Lurra Language and Culture team at Maningrida College. His father's language is Djinang and his mother's language is Wurlaki, both languages belonging to country east of Maningrida. Stanley is part of the Marrangu people who share a songline that stretches from Ritjarrngu country on the Gulf of Carpentaria right up towards the mouth of the Blyth River. Stanley is a ceremonial leader of the Wurrkiganydjarr clan group and performs the songs that are part of this story in ceremonies throughout the Maningrida region.

Then the eagle comes down and tries to scratch the little lizar but his mother gets up really angry._x000d_
Then the little lizard is still asleep and the eagle tries to scratch her baby but the morther of the lizard fights back._x000d_

@graph.name: Ngarra da buth-te ngurrinidha
@graph.description:
A story about camping out bush and hunting. _x000d_
Free translation: _x000d_
1	This story was told to me, from my mother_x000d_
_x000d_
2 & 3  	From the beginning this place, there were people walking around everywhere like butcher bird, blue tongue lizard and the frog.  At first they were people_x000d_
_x000d_
4 & 5  	Then the butcherbird and the crow went together to look around for sugar bag.  They went up the hill top.  The crow said to him “I’ve found a sugar” up in the eucalyptus tree, then the butcher bird said, my brother-in-law found a sugar bag_x000d_
_x000d_
6 & 7  	And the frog came along and said to them.  “Hey you two, can you give me some of you sugar bag please?”  And they answered him we’ve got nothing, because they told him a lie.  And the frog said to them alright then and he kept walking and he said to himself they told me a lie and they said to one another he might finished the sugar bag _x000d_
_x000d_
8 & 9 	He went back walking along and got to the billabong.  He said, “Why didn’t they give some of their sugar bag?”  “oh well, said the frog.  Then the frog went down to where the water was.  The frog began to drink the water, until the water was gone.  When he drank all the water, he went up and sat on top up the hill_x000d_
_x000d_
10 & 11 	Then the crow and the butcherbird got really thirsty.  They ran all along to drink some water.  When they got there they didn’t make a sound flash, but they only walked around and noises of all dead grass.  They started digging for water.  The dirt was all dried._x000d_
_x000d_
12 & 13 	Then the frog called out to them, they looked around and they looked up, there he his and he looks fat sitting on top of the rock.  Then they started calling the others, the crow called when he heard them and the butcherbird called but he didn’t listen.  There were everyone had been hunting, they heard him calling to others, he told them that the frog drank all the water. They told them there’s no water left._x000d_

@graph.name: Ku kananganthan-ka marra-re-ka kadibarlbarldha
@graph.description:
Dreamtime story of why the emu cannot fly. The story was told to Sr Camilla Mary and later published in 'Aboriginal Children's Stories' in English by Kormilda College, Darwin._x000d_
Free translation:_x000d_
1.	The emu had wings.  It was always flying.  He was happy._x000d_
2.	Sometime he use to go down and eat, after that he would go up and fly again._x000d_
3.	He was flying high up.  When he looked down, he saw someone down the ground.  He was flying and got tired. and started to walk, got tired and fell asleep._x000d_
4.	When he was asleep, the old man was looking for something to eat then he saw the bird asleep._x000d_
5.	The old man, jump up and chase the bird, he caught it but it was only wing.  The bird ran off._x000d_
6.	The bird didn’t fly up. but he always walked, that is why the bird doesn’t fly anymore._x000d_

_x000d_
 	Story about a young man who comes into town and spends his money on drinks for his mates. While they are drunk, someone else steals their food. When they wake up, they have no food or money. The man who came into town with the money is left all alone, the others leave him. He is hungry, and ends up stealing food, because no one will look after him. Now he is in jail, how will he learn his language there?

@graph.name: Nginipunh Nhinhi
@graph.subtitle: A Murrinhpatha health dictionary
@graph.description: This community friendly health dictionary covers body parts, face parts, internal organs, hand and foot features, the skeleton and muscles. Accompanying the diagrams are introductory Murrinhpatha conversations for community nurses and patients that assist with assessing basic health issues. To assist non Murrinhpatha speakers, a pronunciation guide and brief of the Murrinhpatha language has been included. This valuable health resource has been developed by Wadeye community members for their clinic and is accompanied by five detailed posters; body parts, the skeleton, the head, internal organs and hand and foot. The book and posters are in Murrinhpatha and English. This is a valuable resource suitable for anyone involved with community health; the community clinic, aged care, child care, primary school, high school and tertiary education.
